title: Parallel lines / intersecting lines: one angle relationship
subtitle: Lines, angles, and triangles · 22 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **22 of the official questions in Lines, angles, and triangles are this one** — 17 Easy, 3 Medium, 2 Hard.
It is bottom-heavy, which makes it cheap points. Secure it early.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- You see a figure with two parallel lines cut by a transversal, or just two crossing lines.
- Two angles are marked, one numeric or both as expressions, and you're asked for a variable.
- The two marked angles are either in matching positions or next to each other on a straight line.
- A harder version has no figure: it describes the eight angles a transversal makes and asks which expression can or cannot equal a sum of four of them.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Name the relationship between the two marked angles: vertical, corresponding, or alternate interior means equal; a linear pair or same-side interior/exterior means they add to 180.
- 2) Write that single equation and solve it.
- 3) For the no-figure version, remember a transversal across parallel lines makes only two distinct angle measures, x and 180 - x.
- Any four of the eight angles sum to a·x + b(180 - x) with a + b = 4.
- Test each choice against that form.

sections.heading: Where Desmos fits
body: Mostly unnecessary, because the equation is one linear step.
If the angles are expressions like 3x + 10 and 5x - 30, you can type each side as y = ... and read the x-value where the lines cross.
For the four-angle-sum version, Desmos doesn't help; you need the structural argument.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You set angles equal when they are actually supplementary, or the reverse.
The wrong choices usually include the other angle's measure, 180 minus the correct answer, or the complement (90 minus the answer).
